files.text:
Wayang kulit

The Shadow Side

A night of puppets cut from buffalo hide, and the lamp that makes them breathe.

Every performance opens and closes with the gunungan, the mountain, which is also called the kayon, the tree. It is a tall leaf of hide, pointed at the top, cut through with a tree of life in which birds perch and monkeys climb, with a bull and a tiger facing each other below and, at its foot, a gate kept by two giants. Before the first scene it stands planted in the middle of the screen. The dalang lifts it, makes it tremble, draws it back toward the lamp until its shadow fills the cloth like a cloud, and brings it in again until every cut is sharp; only then does he lay it aside for the first king to enter. Through the night it returns for whatever the story needs that is not a person: a forest, the sea, a wind, a fire.

The one on this screen comes from Bali, where the kayon is a leaf of flames with a demon’s face at its foot. Javanese gunungan carry the same fire painted red on their backs, and turn it to the audience when a kingdom burns.

A few centimetres of flame

The lamp, the blencong, hangs above the dalang’s head an arm’s length behind the cloth: a bronze vessel of coconut oil, often cast as the bird Garuda, with a fat cotton wick. Its flame is a few centimetres across, and that width is the whole art of the shadow. Pressed to the screen, a figure throws a shadow its own size, and every hole punched in it is a point of light. Drawn back toward the lamp it grows, and its edges spread into a penumbra as wide as the flame, multiplied by the figure’s distance from the screen and divided by its distance from the lamp. A demon held close to the flame fills the screen like weather. And because the flame is never still, the shadow breathes.

Hide, chisel, gold

A puppet begins as the skin of a water buffalo, soaked, stretched on a frame and dried in the sun, then scraped with a blade until it is as thin and stiff as card and lets the light through like horn. The maker draws the figure on it and cuts the outline, then sits with the hide on a block of hardwood and punches it, hour after hour, with a set of small chisels struck by a mallet. Each chisel has its own mouth, a round one for dots, a crescent, a short flat blade, and the patterns they make have names: a chain of tiny diamonds is inten-intenan, little jewels; the saw-toothed fringe along a border is untu walang, grasshopper’s teeth. A fine figure can take weeks of punching before anyone paints it.

Then it is painted on both sides, in layers: a white ground, colours laid on in fine gradations, black lines, gold leaf on the crown, the jewellery and sometimes the skin. A face painted black, gold or red tells the audience the character’s temper before he speaks. A split rod of buffalo horn, warmed and bent, is stitched along the figure from crown to foot and runs on below it as a handle; the arms are jointed at shoulder and elbow and worked by thinner rods from the hands. On the far side of the screen none of the colour shows. What shows is the cutting.

All night

The dalang sits cross-legged behind the screen from about nine in the evening until the sky pales, eight or nine hours, and does not leave it. He works every puppet and speaks every voice: the slow, high courtesy of a knight, the roar of a giant, the jokes of the clown-servants everyone has been waiting for. Between scenes he sings the suluk that set the mood. The puppets not in play stand in ranks along the foot of the screen, their horn rods pushed into the trunks of banana trees, the noble on his right and the wicked on his left. With a wooden mallet in his left hand he knocks on the puppet chest beside him, and with his foot he strikes small metal plates hung on its side; the gamelan behind him takes its cues from both, when to quicken, when to stop, when the fight begins.

Old descriptions disagree about who sat where. Some put the men among the musicians on the dalang’s side, watching the painted figures, and the women on the far side watching shadows; others reverse them. Today most people watch from the dalang’s side, where the colour and the music are, and most performances light the screen with an electric bulb, whose small filament throws a steadier, harder shadow. The oil lamp’s shadow was never still. It brightened and dimmed with the wick, it shivered when the night air moved, and a figure drawn back toward it never quite kept its edges.

At dawn the dalang plants the gunungan in the middle of the screen again, and the play is over.

Tancep kayon

# shadow-puppet Wayang kulit, seen from the shadow side. The element becomes the screen: warm cotton lit from behind by an oil lamp, brightest where it looks into the flame and falling off to orange at the edges, with a dyed red border along the top and the shadow of the banana trunk along the foot. On it is the shadow of a real puppet of punched buffalo hide (a Javanese figure from the Cooper Hewitt and a Balinese fire kayon), the light coming through every hole. Scrolling draws the puppet from the lamp to the screen: a huge, soft shadow that shrinks and sharpens into a crisp lace. Drag moves it, and it leans behind the move and settles back, as a puppet on a horn rod does. The flame flickers, so the shadow breathes, and when the puppet is drawn back it trembles. ```html
``` Or call it yourself: ```js import { shadowPuppet } from './shadow-puppet.js'; const sp = shadowPuppet(el, { src: 'assets/kayon.webp', distance: .5 }); sp.set({ distance: 0 }); // fixed distance, 0 = at the screen, 1 = as far as `far` sp.state; // { distance, magnification, lean, grip, flame, live, running } sp(); // destroy: canvas, GL, listeners, observers, loop ``` Give the element a size; the canvas fills it. The `` is what shows without JS or WebGL: the same image turned black by a CSS filter, holes and all, on a warm gradient panel with the bands. Set the `--sp-*` variables to the same numbers as the data attributes so it stands where the live shadow will. ## Options On the element (`data-*`) or in the options object, which wins. | attribute | option | default | | |---|---|---|---| | `data-src` | `src` | the inner img | the puppet: an RGBA image, alpha = hide, holes transparent, as seen from the audience (mirrored). Same origin | | `data-height` | `height` | `1` | the image's height at the screen, in screen heights (it includes the rod) | | `data-top` | `top` | `.06` | where its top sits at the screen, of the screen's height | | `data-at` | `at` | `.5` | across, of the screen's width | | `data-grip` | `grip` | `.5 1` | the rod's end in the image (u v): the hand, and the pivot of the lean | | `data-scroll` | `scroll` | none | a selector (an ancestor or any element) whose scroll-through draws the puppet in. Without it, it arrives as the screen's middle reaches the middle of the view | | `data-reach` | `reach` | `.78` | the share of that scroll it takes to reach the screen (then it stays) | | `data-far` | `far` | `.62` | how far back toward the lamp it starts, as a share of the lamp's distance. Capped on narrow screens so the shadow stays about the screen's width | | `data-lamp` | `lamp` | `.5 .3` | the foot of the flame on the screen | | `data-depth` | `depth` | `1.15` | lamp to screen, in screen heights | | `data-flame` | `flame` | `.05` | the flame's width, in screen heights (the penumbra scales with it) | | `data-glow` | `glow` | `.05` | how much lamplight the hide lets through, tinted by the paint | | `data-flicker` | `flicker` | `1` | 0 = a perfectly steady flame | | `data-sway` | `sway` | `1` | how much it leans behind a quick move | | `data-seams` | `seams` | `.34 .69` | where the cotton widths are sewn (fractions of the width); `0 0` for none | | `data-seed` | `seed` | `3` | the weave and the flame's rhythm | ## How it works - **Projection.** The lamp is a small flame at distance `D` behind the screen; the puppet is flat, parallel to it, at distance `d` from the screen. A puppet point `P` lands at `s = L + (P − L)·M` with `M = D / (D − d)`, so the shadow grows about the foot of the lamp, not about the puppet. Each pixel runs this backwards, then undoes the puppet's lean about the grip, and reads the puppet. - **Penumbra.** A flame of width `F` blurs every edge by `F·d / (D − d)`: zero at the screen, wider than a hand when the puppet is held back. The flame is half again as tall as it is wide, so the blur is too, and vertical edges stay sharper than horizontal ones. The blur is a stack: the alpha, then blurred by ellipses of radius 1, 2, 4 … 64 texels (64-tap Vogel spirals, each level from the last), packed four to an RGBA texture. A pixel interpolates the two levels around its radius, plus half a device pixel of footprint so the crisp lace never aliases. The drag also follows the projection: the hand moves `1/M` as far as the finger, so the shadow stays under it. - **Light.** The screen's brightness is the cos³ fall-off of a point source, `(D² / (D² + r²))^1.5`, plus a hot spot where the cloth looks into the flame, times a coconut-oil flame's colour (about 1900 K), through a filmic shoulder `1 − e^(−2.15x)`, so the centre goes pale gold and the edges deep orange. - **Hide.** The puppet is rawhide scraped thin, so a little light gets through it: the paint's colour, read from a blurred mip of the image (blurred further so the photograph's own lighting stays out), adds `glow` × colour inside the shadow. - **Holes blaze.** The hide is opaque, so the half-tones the downsampled texture leaves in small punches are pushed back to open while the shadow is crisp: each hole passes the lamp undimmed, as bright as the open cloth beside it. A hair of bloom (the stack read two css px wider) lets the light spill round them, so the lace sparkles at the hot spot. - **Cloth.** A fine, even over-and-under weave about a css pixel apart (laid out in device pixels so it never beats with them, 2.6% contrast, its threads wandering a little), now and then a slub thread running thick and a little darker for a long way, a cloudy density in three scales, a little sag, two seams with a fold of light, red dyed bands at top and bottom lit through, the frame's shadow at the sides and the banana trunk's shadow at the foot, where the rod disappears as rods do. - **Flame.** Four octaves of smooth noise for brightness, size and a sway of the flame's position, and every 4-10 s a draught that lays it over for a second or two. Moving the flame by `δ` moves the shadow by `δ·(1 − M)`: still at the screen, a tremble when held back. Brightness, softness and the hot spot all breathe with it. - **The hand.** The grip follows its target on a stiff critically damped spring; its acceleration drives a damped spring for the lean (ω 6.2 rad/s, ζ 0.26), so the puppet's top lags a quick move, swings past, and settles. When nothing is held, the hand drifts by a fraction of a percent and the puppet is never quite still. ## The images Each puppet is one RGBA image, 1024 × 2048 (power-of-two, for the paint's mipmaps), mirrored, with the rod's end at the bottom centre. They were cut out of museum photographs at full resolution (the script is not part of the component): the figure lies flat on white paper, so the backdrop is bright and grey and the holes show the dark paper in the puppet's own contact shadow, darker than any paint; the kayon stands against a wall, so wall and holes are told from the copper hide by blue over red, and broad glare patches that read as holes are refilled. A 5-7 px median cleans the outline. The kayon's rod leaves the photograph, so it is carried on in its own colour. ## Theming The screen has no theme colours: it is lamplight on cotton. Style the element's size, frame and margins freely (the demo gives it a wooden frame with `box-shadow`). `--sp-at`, `--sp-top`, `--sp-height` place the no-script still; `--accent` colours the focus ring. Keep the room around it warm and not black: the demo uses a dusk paper tone with a glow. ## Accessibility and reduced motion - The element is focusable with a label (yours if you give one); arrow keys move the puppet (Shift for bigger steps). The canvas is `aria-hidden`; the images are decorative. - `touch-action: pan-y`: on a phone a vertical swipe scrolls the page and a sideways drag moves the puppet. With a mouse, drag moves it both ways. - `prefers-reduced-motion: reduce`: a still frame with the puppet at the screen, crisp, and the flame at rest. Nothing moves by itself; dragging still works (it redraws once per move, no sway). The demo drops its tall scroll sections. ## Cost - One full-canvas draw at 30 fps while the screen is on screen (the flame always moves); nothing off screen (IntersectionObserver) or in a hidden tab. - DPR capped at 2, and 4.6 Mpx a frame at most. Per pixel: two stack reads, one mip read, a little noise for the cloth. - Once per puppet: eight full-texture blur passes on the GPU (about 128 Mtap, a few tens of ms), three 8 MB textures kept. - Assets: 205 KB figure, 253 KB kayon, 176 KB painted figure for the essay. - If the GPU drops the context the canvas goes and the still shows until it comes back. ## Credits - Shadow puppet (wayang kulit), Java, 19th century. Cooper Hewitt, Smithsonian Design Museum, 1935-15-1. Smithsonian Open Access, CC0. - Fire Kayon, wayang kulit, Bali.
